definition: A sacred K'iche' Maya narrative of creation, the Hero Twins and the first people, written down in the 16th century and known today from a later manuscript copy. Its name is often translated as 'Book of the Council' or 'Book of the Community'.
A Maya people of the highlands of Guatemala and their language, in which the Popol Vuh was written down; K'iche' is still spoken by many people today.
The underworld, or place of the dead, in K'iche' tradition, ruled by a council of lords who test and challenge the visitors who come down to it.
The council of death gods who rule Xibalba, led by Hun Came (One Death) and Vucub Came (Seven Death); they summon the ballplayers in the Popol Vuh.
Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the twin brothers of the Popol Vuh who defeat Seven Macaw and the lords of Xibalba. They are among the most important figures in Maya tradition.
Corn, the staple crop of Mesoamerica and a sacred substance in Maya tradition; in the Popol Vuh the first true people are made from maize dough.
A Mesoamerican game played with a heavy rubber ball on a stone court, often carrying religious and political meaning. The story of the Hero Twins begins with a ball game.
A book of folded bark paper or deer hide painted by Maya scribes. Only four pre-conquest Maya codices survive, though colonial accounts describe many more.
A Maya title meaning 'lord' or 'ruler', and also the name of a day in the Maya calendar. The word appears in the names and titles of many kings.
A spirit companion or animal co-essence in many Maya communities, and in some highland towns a ritual specialist. The meaning varies from place to place.
